newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Zimbabwe's Mugabe champions trade in African ivory.
newsitem.headline: Zimbabwe's Mugabe champions trade in African ivory.

text.p: Zimbabwe, one of the key champions of a controversial proposal to resume trade in African ivory, urged the world community on Monday to reward sustainable wildlife management or face certain environmental disaster.

Officially opening a 10-day Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species (CITES), Zimbabwe President Robert Mugabe said the international community must not deprive countries access to their natural wealth.
Elephant-rich Zimbabwe, Namibia, and Botswana are sponsoring a proposal at the CITES conference for a partial lifting of a seven-year-old ban on ivory sales.

The three countries and their supporters, notably Japan, say they must be allowed some limited but strictly supervised trade because their elephant herd, now estimated at around 150,000, is rising steadily and was doing so even before the 1989 ban.

Since the ban was imposed they have accumulated nearly 100 tonnes of ivory from annual culls and from legally hunted trophies. They say that trade in ivory is vital to stabilise the elephant herd, which they say is now over twice the land's carrying capacity.

"There must be encouragement of sustainable utilisation and development for those whose policies and actions uphold scientifically accepted standards, while penalising those that abuse the environment," Mugabe said to applause, mainly from the Zimbabwean contigent among the more than 2,000 delegates and observers at the CITES meeting.
"To refuse to accept the principle of differentiated responsibilities will mean doom for the environmental movement and certainly disaster to natural resources covered by CITES convention," he said.
Mugabe said wildlife in Southern Africa was mostly found in arid and semi-desert regions where water was expensive to pump.
"Elephants, especially because of their huge bodies, consume large amounts of this underground water and, we believe, every species must pay its way to survival," he said.
Debate on the ivory trade ban is expected to dominate the CITES conference which is considering nearly 80 proposals.

The proposal to allow ivory sales is strongly opposed by some influential green movements and countries, including the U.S.-based African Elephant Foundation, and the United States and French governments. They argue lifting the ban will leave elephants at the mercy of poachers.

The 138-member CITES will vote on the issue towards the end of the 10-day conference, but Amsterdam-based environment group Greenpeace says it will campaign for an open ballot to minimise the possibilities of governments taking positions not backed by their domestic constituencies.
CITES Secretary-General Ezgrev Topkov urged the conference to be level-headed, saying it would achieve more that way.
The conference is also expected to generate intense debate on a proposal by Japan and Norway to open up whale hunting.
Greenpeace spokeswoman Isabel McCrea told a press briefing the the threat to whales was real, accusing both Norway and Japan of trading support with countries that backed their proposals.

The meeting will also debate ways to preserve the Indian tiger, the black rhino, the sturgeon fish and the Cuban sea turtle -- all threatened by poachers. CITES estimates the illegal global trade in endangered species is worth up to $10 billion a year.
